data:
How do we reason about reason? Are there underlying principles that can connect reasoning about philosophical abstractions, legal and politics argument, analysis of texts, scientific and social scientific theorisations, solving puzzles and writing mathematical proofs? Can we make precise what we mean by reason or codify what we mean by a reasonable argument? How have philosophers lent meaning to make sense of the human quest to discover the laws of reason?

This course attempts to trace the long standing intellectual project of identifying the laws of deductive reasoning. We begin with historical attempts and philosophical underpinnings underlying these attempts, before diving deep into contemporary formal frameworks that fall under the aegis of logic.

In the process, we use precise formulations of deductive reasoning using symbolic abstractions which enables us to answer the following questions:

How do we ensure that a set of sentences are mutually consistent?
How do we make sense of paradoxes?
How do we ensure that deductive arguments are logically sound?
What can and cannot be deduced from a given collection of statements?
How do we reason precisely when confronted with ambiguities such as knowledge or lack of it, and belief and contingency?

We further extend our set of questions to attempt to answer the following questions about the method of reasoning itself:

What kind of statements are amenable to formal deductive reasoning?
What is the nature of the relationship between reasoning and language?
How do we reason within a given formal reasoning system as well as about a given formal reasoning system?

The course intends to provide access to ideas and contemporary vocabulary which will enable to deploy logic as a means to reason within philosophy, as well as enable pursuit logic and philosophy of logic as philosophical disciplines. Further it will bring alive challenges which makes the process of sound reasoning difficult even for sophisticated Artificial Intelligence tools today.
